summary: The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek hand-powered model of the Solar System, built in the 2nd century BC. It is the oldest known analogue computer. It predicted astronomical positions and eclipses decades ahead and tracked the cycle of the ancient Olympic Games. It was recovered in 1901 from the wreck of a Roman cargo ship off the Greek island of Antikythera. Its gears went unnoticed until 1902, when Valerios and Spyridon Stais saw one in a corroded lump at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, where its 82 fragments are kept. Scans in 2005 showed about 35 bronze gears that followed the Sun and Moon, predicted eclipses and modelled the Moon's uneven orbit. Its date and origin are debated. Proposed dates run from about 205 BC to 87 BC, and the ship sank around 70 to 60 BC. Machines of similar complexity did not appear again until 14th-century Europe.
